title: Desert Survivors
objective: After this level you can explain how camels and other animals survive with little water.
summary: A camel's hump is fat, not water; it drinks up to about 30 gallons at once and can go nearly a week without. A kangaroo rat gets water from dry seeds and wastes almost none.

cards.headline: A camel's hump holds no water at all.
cards.body: It's fat. So how does a desert animal get enough water, and hang on to it? The desert has two famous answers, one very large and one very small.

cards.headline: The camel: fill up, then go
cards.body: The hump is a food store: fat to live on when food is scarce. Packing the fat into one hump also means the rest of the body isn't wrapped in insulation in the heat. Water is a separate trick. A camel can drink up to about 30 gallons (about 114 liters) in one sitting, then go nearly a week without drinking. It doesn't carry a tank. It just refills like a bathtub.

cards.headline: The kangaroo rat: barely drink at all
cards.body: A kangaroo rat eats mostly dry seeds, yet it has almost no need to drink. Digesting a gram of seeds gives it about half a gram of water, roughly one drop for every two seeds. Its breakfast is also its water bottle.

cards.headline: Spend almost nothing
cards.body: Making water only works if you don't waste it. A kangaroo rat neither sweats nor pants, and its kidneys concentrate its urine to an almost crystal-like consistency. It also spends the hot day in its burrow and comes out at night. The camel refills big; the kangaroo rat hardly spends any.

cards.headline: Desert survivors: explained
learned: A camel's hump is fat, not water
Camels drink up to about 30 gallons at once
Kangaroo rats get water from dry seeds
No sweating, no panting, very concentrated urine
Burrow by day, out at night

options.label: It stores extra water in its long tail
